tagline: Ebenezer Baptist pastor for 44 years, Atlanta voting-rights leader, and father of Martin Luther King Jr.
burial: Martin Luther King Sr. is buried at South-View Cemetery beside his wife Alberta Williams King, beneath a combined marker near the front gates. Reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution; Find a Grave places the plot next to First Road, paralleling Jonesboro Road.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. was born Michael King on December 19, 1899, in Stockbridge, Georgia, the eldest son of James and Delia King. (The Stanford King Institute gives 1897; see Where sources disagree.) In 1918 Michael King left Stockbridge for Atlanta, joining his sister Woodie there. On Thanksgiving Day 1926 he married Alberta Christine Williams at Ebenezer Baptist Church, where her father, Rev. A. D. Williams, was pastor. The couple had three children: Willie Christine (born 1927), Michael Luther Jr., later known as Martin Luther King Jr. (born 1929), and Alfred Daniel Williams (born 1930). Michael King later changed his own name, and the name of his eldest son, to Martin Luther King. He outlived his wife and both of his sons.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. had limited schooling as a boy, attending the Stockbridge Colored School for only three to five months a year. After moving to Atlanta he studied at Bryant Preparatory School, and in 1926 he was admitted to Morehouse College, where he earned a bachelor's degree in theology. The Stanford King Institute indicates he received that degree around 1930, shortly before the birth of his son A. D.; other accounts give 1931 (see Where sources disagree). In 1975 Dillard University awarded Martin Luther King Sr. an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. pastored several churches in College Park, Georgia, in the early 1920s while he was still studying. In 1931 he succeeded his father-in-law, Rev. A. D. Williams, as pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, and he served Ebenezer for 44 years in all. In 1934 he attended the Baptist World Alliance meeting in Berlin. He served on the boards of Atlanta University, Morehouse College and the National Baptist Convention. In 1964 he traveled to Oslo, Norway, for the ceremony at which his son Martin Luther King Jr. received the Nobel Peace Prize. A strong supporter of Jimmy Carter, Martin Luther King Sr. delivered invocations at the Democratic National Conventions of 1976 and 1980.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. was a local leader in the NAACP and in the Atlanta Civic and Political League. In 1935 he joined other ministers of the Atlanta Baptist Ministers Union in calling for Black voter registration, and on March 6, 1936, he spoke at an NAACP mass meeting at Wheat Street Baptist Church. He is widely reported to have led a voting-rights march on Atlanta City Hall in 1936; the Stanford King Institute instead describes a 1939 proposal for a voter registration drive beginning with a march to City Hall. He personally defied segregation, for example by riding the whites-only City Hall elevator to reach the voter registrar. In 1940 he chaired the Committee on the Equalization of Teachers' Salaries, a campaign that, with NAACP legal help, brought significant gains for Black teachers. During the Montgomery bus boycott, Martin Luther King Sr. unsuccessfully urged his son not to return to Montgomery.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. became widely known as "Daddy King," the name he used for the title of his 1980 autobiography, Daddy King: An Autobiography. His 44 years in the pulpit of Ebenezer Baptist Church, his early work for Black voter registration in Atlanta and his campaign to equalize teachers' salaries made him a civic leader in his own right, not only the father of Martin Luther King Jr. Dillard University recognized him with an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters in 1975. Martin Luther King Sr. died in Atlanta on November 11, 1984, having outlived his wife Alberta and both of his sons, and he rests beside Alberta at South-View Cemetery.

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Martin Luther King Sr. was born Michael King and later changed both his own name and his eldest son's name to Martin Luther King. He was pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church for 44 years, beginning in 1931. He gave the invocation at the 1976 and 1980 Democratic National Conventions. He outlived his wife and both sons and is buried beside Alberta King under a combined marker at South-View. Martin Luther King Jr. was also first buried at South-View after his assassination in April 1968, before being moved about two years later to the King Center tomb on Auburn Avenue.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources differ on several points about Martin Luther King Sr. Birth year: the Stanford King Institute says he was born December 19, 1897, while Find a Grave, Wikipedia and the Civil Rights Digital Library authority record give 1899; his reported age of 84 at death also fits 1899, so this profile uses 1899. City Hall march: Find a Grave and a report attributed to 11Alive say he led Atlanta's first Black voting-rights march, on City Hall, in 1936, while the Stanford King Institute describes a 1939 proposal for a registration drive starting with a City Hall march; these may be two separate events. Cause of death: Wikipedia, citing a New York Times obituary that could not be checked, says he died of a heart attack at Crawford W. Long Hospital, whereas a cemetery travel blog says he died after a stroke; Stanford gives no cause. Morehouse degree: Stanford implies he finished his theology degree around 1930, while Wikipedia says he began in 1925 and earned a Bachelor of Theology in 1931.

tagline: Ebenezer Baptist organist for 40 years and choir founder, mother of Martin Luther King Jr.
burial: Alberta Williams King is buried at South-View Cemetery with her husband, Martin Luther King Sr., beneath a combined marker near the front gates. Reported by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution; Find a Grave records the inscription "...Her Life Shall Be Filled With Music...".

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Alberta Williams King was born Alberta Christine Williams on September 13, 1903, in Atlanta, according to the Stanford King Institute (Find a Grave gives 1904). Alberta Williams was the only surviving child of Jennie Celeste Williams and Rev. Adam Daniel (A. D.) Williams, pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church. Her parents are also buried at South-View Cemetery, along with two of their children who died in infancy. On Thanksgiving Day 1926 she married Michael King, who later took the name Martin Luther King Sr. and succeeded her father as Ebenezer's pastor. The couple had three children: Willie Christine, Martin Luther King Jr. and Alfred Daniel.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: Alberta Williams King attended Spelman Seminary for high school and then earned a teaching certificate from Hampton Normal and Industrial Institute in Virginia. She taught briefly but had to stop because the local school board did not allow married women to teach. Years later, as a married mother of three, Alberta Williams King completed a bachelor's degree at Morris Brown College in Atlanta in 1938.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: Alberta Williams King served as organist at Ebenezer Baptist Church from 1932 to 1972, a span of 40 years, and she founded the Ebenezer choir. From 1950 to 1962 she was also organist for the Women's Auxiliary of the National Baptist Convention. Beyond music, Alberta Williams King was active in community and reform organizations, including the YWCA, the NAACP and the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom. Her work at the organ and with the choir made music a central part of worship at Ebenezer for four decades, during which her husband and later her sons served in its pulpit.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: Alberta Williams King was shot during Sunday services at Ebenezer Baptist Church on June 30, 1974, while she was playing the organ, and died later that day. The gunman, Marcus Chenault of Ohio, claimed that "All Christians are my enemies." According to news reports, she was playing "The Lord's Prayer"; deacon Edward Boykin was also killed and congregant Jimmie Mitchell was wounded. Chenault's original target was reportedly Martin Luther King Sr.; he claimed insanity but was convicted and sentenced to death. Her death came six years after her son Martin Luther King Jr. was assassinated. Alberta Williams King is remembered at South-View, where her gravestone reads "...Her Life Shall Be Filled With Music...".

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: Alberta Williams King was killed at the organ of Ebenezer Baptist Church on June 30, 1974, six years after her son's assassination. She played the organ at Ebenezer for 40 years, from 1932 to 1972, and founded its choir. Her gravestone at South-View reads "...Her Life Shall Be Filled With Music...". Her father, A. D. Williams, was Ebenezer's pastor before her husband, and her parents are also buried at South-View. She earned her bachelor's degree from Morris Brown College in 1938, as a married mother of three.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: Sources disagree on Alberta Williams King's birth year and age. The Stanford King Institute says she was born September 13, 1903, and died at age 70, while Find a Grave gives September 13, 1904, and an age of 69 at death, and Wikipedia and other outlets also report 69. Each pair of figures is internally consistent; this profile uses the Stanford date as the more authoritative source. Sources also differ on the age of her killer, Marcus Chenault: Stanford gives 21, while Wikipedia reportedly gives 23.

tagline: Baptist pastor and civil rights activist, younger brother of Martin Luther King Jr.
burial: A.D. King is buried at South-View Cemetery, according to a cemetery travel blog and Wikipedia's list of South-View burials. Our research found no obituary or plot location confirming it.

sections.heading: Early life and family
sections.text: Alfred Daniel Williams King, known as "A. D." to family and friends, was born July 30, 1930, in Atlanta, the son of Alberta Williams King and Martin Luther King Sr. A.D. King was the younger brother of Martin Luther King Jr., his only brother, and of Willie Christine King (later Farris). On June 17, 1950, A.D. King married Naomi Barber, and the couple had five children. Their daughter Alveda, born in 1951, was the first King grandchild. Their son Vernon died in 2009 at age 49.

sections.heading: Education
sections.text: A.D. King married Naomi Barber as a teenager, in 1950, before he attended college. He initially resisted entering the ministry, but during the 1950s he assisted his father at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta. A.D. King went on to graduate from Morehouse College in 1959, the same year he took up his first pastorate, at Mount Vernon First Baptist Church in Newnan, Georgia.

sections.heading: Career and achievements
sections.text: A.D. King served as pastor of Mount Vernon First Baptist Church in Newnan, Georgia, beginning in 1959. He then moved to Alabama to lead First Street Baptist Church in Ensley, near Birmingham; the Stanford King Institute dates this to 1963, while the Atlanta Journal-Constitution says 1961. In 1965 A.D. King became pastor of Zion Baptist Church in Louisville, Kentucky. In September 1968, months after his brother's assassination, he was installed as co-pastor of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta alongside his father.

sections.heading: Civil rights and civic life
sections.text: A.D. King was arrested with his brother Martin Luther King Jr. and about 70 others at an Atlanta lunch-counter sit-in in October 1960. In 1963 he was a leader of the Birmingham Campaign and was arrested several times. On May 11, 1963, the Saturday before Mother's Day, his Birmingham home was bombed; a second bomb collapsed the front of the house after the family had left the front room. In August 1963, after the bombing of a Black lawyer's home set off rioting, A.D. King climbed onto a car and told the crowd, "If you're going to kill someone, then kill me...." In Louisville he formed the Kentucky Christian Leadership Conference and fought for fair housing, winning an open-housing ordinance in 1968. On April 4, 1968, he was at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, in the room beneath his brother's. Afterward he was mentioned as a possible SCLC leader but did not pursue it, staying active in the Poor People's Campaign.

sections.heading: Legacy and honors
sections.text: A.D. King died on July 21, 1969, at age 38, about 15 months after his brother's assassination. He was found at the bottom of the swimming pool at his Atlanta home by his son Derek, the morning after a July 20 phone call, while his wife Naomi was vacationing in Jamaica. His death was officially ruled an accidental drowning. Some family members have disputed that ruling (see Where sources disagree). His widow, Naomi King, later founded the A.D. King Foundation with Atlanta Metropolitan State College professor Babs Onabanjo, and his life is the subject of the 2009 documentary "A.D. King: Brother to the Dreamer."

sections.heading: Did you know?
sections.text: A.D. King was Martin Luther King Jr.'s only brother, and his daughter Alveda King was the first King grandchild. His Birmingham home was bombed on May 11, 1963. He won a campaign for an open-housing ordinance in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1968. He was at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis when his brother was assassinated on April 4, 1968. A.D. King died about 15 months later, on July 21, 1969, when he was found in his home swimming pool.

sections.heading: Where sources disagree
sections.text: A.D. King's death on July 21, 1969, was officially ruled an accidental drowning. Members of his family dispute that ruling: according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, his widow Naomi King said, "Absolutely, he was murdered," and his daughter Alveda King said, "Daddy was killed and put in the pool." Andrew Young, by contrast, told the newspaper he believed A.D. King had a heart attack and that "There was never any evidence of foul play." Sources also differ on smaller details. His age at death is 38 according to the Stanford King Institute and the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, which matches his birth date, but a cemetery travel blog says 39. Stanford dates his move to Ensley, Alabama, to 1963, while the Atlanta Journal-Constitution says 1961. The newspaper lists his children as Alveda, Alfred, Derek, Esther and Vernon, while Wikipedia lists Alveda, Alfred Jr., Derek, Darlene and Vernon.
